Severe pain during periods is not a routine menstrual symptom and should be medically evaluated. One common underlying cause is endometriosis, a condition in which menstrual blood flows backward through the fallopian tubes into the abdominal cavity instead of flowing out normally. This backward flow leads to inflammation and significant pelvic pain, especially during menstruation. This pain, known as dysmenorrhea, can be severe enough to interfere with daily activities.

With repeated cycles, this condition can result in the formation of ovarian cysts filled with old blood, commonly referred to as chocolate cysts. These cysts are frequently identified on pelvic sonography and usually indicate a long-standing or chronic form of endometriosis.

Endometriosis is not limited to pain alone. Over time, it can affect ovarian function, ovulation, and the pelvic environment, and may contribute to fertility challenges in some women. Early clinical assessment and imaging help in identifying the condition and planning appropriate management.

At Aadityacare Maternity Hospital, Bhandup, evaluation of severe period pain focuses on identifying the underlying cause and addressing it in a timely and structured manner.

Infertility is defined as the inability to conceive after 12 months of regular, unprotected intercourse. It is classified as primary infertility when there has been no previous pregnancy, and secondary infertility when conception does not occur after an earlier childbirth. Both require proper medical evaluation and should not be dismissed as age or stress related alone.

In a normal menstrual cycle, an egg is selected from one ovary in the early phase of the cycle. This egg matures over the next several days and is released during ovulation, usually around the mid-cycle period. Fertilisation occurs in the fallopian tube when sperm meets the egg. The fertilised egg then travels to the uterus, where implantation in the endometrial lining leads to pregnancy.

When ovulation is irregular, egg quality is compromised, fertilisation does not occur, or implantation is inadequate, pregnancy may not happen despite regular cycles and intercourse. A significant proportion of infertility cases are linked to ovulatory dysfunction, hormonal imbalance, or timing issues within the menstrual cycle.
